Cancer genes and survival
Plain language Technical

An audit of 33 questions about tumour DNA and survival

What the tumour records say, and what they only seem to say

Nineteen hospitals have pooled the DNA tests of a quarter of a million tumours into a public project called GENIE. For some of those patients, nurses and doctors also went through the charts and recorded every treatment and how long each person lived. We used that data to test 33 questions of one form: does a particular change in a tumour's genes go with living longer or shorter?

Counts cover the 33 questions in the original plan. Three bonus checks on an extra dataset are included below.

How to read the curves on this page

Every chart here is a survival curve. Start at the left: 100% of a group is alive. Move right through the months and the line steps down each time someone dies. Small tick marks are patients who were still alive when the records end. Where a line crosses 50% is the group's typical (median) survival. Hover or tap on a chart to read off the exact numbers.

Below, lung-cancer patients with and without a change in the EGFR gene. The EGFR line stays higher the whole way: more of those patients were alive at every point.

The p-value in the corner is the chance of a gap at least this large arising if the two groups were really the same. Below 0.05 is the usual bar; below 0.001 is convincing.

The trap that fooled several of the original slides

Some questions compared patients who had a treatment, or a second biopsy, with patients who did not. That sounds fair but hides a trap: to be in the treated group you first have to live long enough to get the treatment. Counting survival from the original diagnosis then gives the treated group a head start that has nothing to do with the treatment. Statisticians call it immortal time.

Brain-tumour patients whose sample was taken after temozolomide seem to live twice as long. Switch to counting from the day the sample was taken and the picture reverses: these are patients whose tumour came back, and they did worse.

Four of the six slide results marked "replicate" turned out to be this trap. They are labelled An illusion below.

What recurs across every cancer

  • TP53 is the bad partner everywhere. In lung, breast, prostate and ALK-fusion tumours, adding a TP53 change to the main driver cut survival by a third to a half. It is the one gene that passed the statistical bar in dataset after dataset.
  • Losing the CDKN2A/B genes matters. It halved survival in bladder cancer and shortened it in pancreatic, ALK-fusion lung and glioblastoma patients.
  • Treatment comparisons need treatment dates. Every slide that compared treated with untreated patients from diagnosis overstated the benefit. Counting from the day the drug started removed it each time.
  • The DNA test itself can mislead. How often a gene change is found depends on which test the hospital used (the ERG rearrangement in prostate cancer ranges from 0% to 33% by test). Comparisons only count patients whose test could have found the change.

Glossary

Mutation, deletion, amplification, fusion

Four ways a gene can change in a tumour. A mutation is a spelling change in the gene. A deep deletion means both copies of the gene are gone. An amplification means many extra copies. A fusion is a rearrangement that joins two genes into one, often switching one of them permanently on (EML4-ALK in lung, TMPRSS2-ERG in prostate).

Median survival

The time by which half the group had died. It is used instead of the average because many patients are still alive when the records stop, so the average cannot be computed.

Hazard ratio (HR)

How much faster one group's risk of death runs than another's. HR 2 means twice the risk at any moment; HR 0.5 means half. On the technical page every comparison carries one, with a range in which the true value probably lies.

Why "statistical bar" and not just "bigger number"

When you test hundreds of genes at once, some will look important by chance. The analysis corrects for this (a method called false-discovery-rate control) so that a gene labelled "holds up" is one unlikely to be a fluke.

Immortal time

The time a patient must survive to qualify for a group, during which they could not have died while counted in that group. Counting it in their favour exaggerates any benefit. The fix is to start the clock at the moment of qualification (the treatment start or the biopsy).

Where the patients come from

Memorial Sloan Kettering, Dana-Farber, Vanderbilt and Princess Margaret for the detailed cohorts; nineteen cancer centres in North America and Europe for the main GENIE database. All are academic hospitals, so the patients are not a cross-section of everyone with cancer.

Data: AACR Project GENIE (BPC cohorts and the v20.0-public release, via Synapse) and genie.cbioportal.org (AKT1, DFCI glioma and DFCI metastatic breast studies). Analysis code, notebooks and tables: explore-genie. Built by Daniel Feller with Claude Code, October 2026.

These are statistical associations in past patients from a handful of academic hospitals. They are not predictions for any individual and not treatment advice.
